title: As Though It Mattered: Hollywood, AI and the End of Original Ideas
author: Peter Bach
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/Sunset_Boulevard_ad_-_18_Aug_1950-680x605.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/15/as-
though-it-mattered-hollywood-ai-and-the-end-of-original-ideas/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/Sunset_Boulevard_ad_-_18_Aug_1950-680x605.jpg)

Theatrical advertisement from 1950 - Public Domain

I am not entirely up to speed on what the feature film business in London is
like these days, but I do remember a production meeting for _28 Days Later._

There were department heads around a large table, Andrew Macdonald at the
helm. There is a particular atmosphere to those meetings—everyone present, but
not entirely there, each waiting for their moment to speak, or not to, as
though something important were taking place.

It struck me, even then, that nothing in the room had quite begun anywhere.

At one point someone turned—I was head of post-production, or something
similarly digital in a field still finding its legs—and barked an order at me.

“No one has spoken to me like that since school,” I said.

The room went quiet. Not because I had said anything especially provocative,
but because I had said anything at all.

What stayed with me was not the tone, but the assumption behind it—that this
was how things were done, and that it mattered.

My first contact with the film world had come years earlier, when Alan Parker
was making  _Pink Floyd – The Wall._ I met a young American woman in
London—she was playing a groupie. I was young myself. We hung out at Blake’s
Hotel in Kensington, surrounded by a high level of ease and access that felt
staged.

“It’s all acting,” she said.

At the time, I took that to mean the obvious. Later, I wondered if she meant
everything else, too. The way people conversed about films, about books, about
each other. There was a second-hand quality to it all, as though everything
had already been said somewhere else and was now being repeated with
surprising conviction.

In the immediate years that followed, I moved through very different
environments—filming alone in a war zone, later working in two New York
galleries where the question of whether something meant anything at all was
treated with near-oppressive seriousness.

Set against those experiences, the film world seemed to operate according to a
different logic altogether. Not frivolous, exactly, but curiously unanchored.
It was as though the relationship between idea and origin had loosened
somehow. Ideas did not need to come from anywhere in particular. They just
needed to circulate convincingly once they appeared.

I saw this most clearly in Los Angeles. There—actors, producers, the already
canonised dead hovering in the background—everything arrived with a prior
life. It wasn’t that the ideas were particularly bad. It was just that they
seemed to arrive pre-assembled. Everything was a form of regurgitation.

At the Chateau Marmont—where I stayed in the bungalow where John Belushi
died—there was a constant exchange of fragments. I saw scripts passed around,
projects half-described over drinks. Dean Stockwell floated in the pool with a
cigar like a ship’s funnel. Elsewhere, producers and actors spoke in
references—this meets that, with a touch of something else. Nothing was just
what it was.

At a party at Roland Joffé’s house—he was away filming, the house lent to
friends—people dive-bombed into the pool while conversations drifted from one
project to another. A friendly Alan Rickman circulated. Scripts moved from
hand to hand—not as works in progress, but as already-legible combinations, as
though their meaning had been decided elsewhere. Everything was in motion.

What still seemed missing was any clear sense of where ideas began. I was
writing a script with a friend and even we didn’t know.

It wasn’t that nothing existed. It was that everything felt weightless—ideas
assembled out of other ideas, passed around until no one quite knew where they
had come from.

And yet everyone behaved as though they mattered enormously.

I accept that this is not unique to Hollywood, though Hollywood made it
visible. Any system that depends on constant novelty will probably eventually
learn to simulate it. References replace influences. Influences replace
experience. Over time, the distinction between drawing from something and just
rearranging it a bit begins to blur.

What matters, then, is not whether something is original in any strict sense—a
question that has always been difficult to answer—but whether it carries any
“necessity”. Whether it feels as though it had to be made, rather than merely
could be.

That was the quality I found missing, even then. Not originality, exactly, but
urgency.

More importantly now, that is what makes the current conversation about AI
feel for me slightly misplaced.

We always insist on framing it as a question of origin—what comes from the
machine, what comes from the human—as though that distinction will tell us
something meaningful or important. But the erosion—the chipping away—of origin
was already well underway. The problem is not the machine. It is the idea
itself.

Or rather, the absence of it.

AI does not introduce this condition. It removes the last obstacles that
allowed it to go unnoticed.

Originality is about where something comes from. Urgency is about why it
exists at all. The two are often confused, but they are not the same.

It is the difference between something that can be instantly recognised and
something that takes time to register—something that resists being reduced to
‘this meets that.’

You can see it most plainly in what these systems are actually sold as doing.
When systems like Grok offer to turn sketches into “live-action” scenes, they
are performing the same trick I saw years ago in hotel bars and swimming
pools. This is taking something insubstantial and dressing it up until it
resembles meaning.

What has changed is that it no longer holds.

For a long time, the distance between an idea and its expression—between the
vague suggestion and the finished film—allowed a certain ambiguity to persist.
Mystery was bestowed. It could even be enjoyed. Effort could be mistaken for
depth. Scale for substance. The machinery of production gave even the most
derivative combinations a kind of gravitational pull, a satisfying tweak. They
felt as though they must have come from somewhere.

AI collapses that distance. It produces something recognisably “finished”
almost immediately, without the visible labour or hard graft that once helped
sustain belief or kept the audience “gripped”. What might once have passed
through many hands, a vast number of rewrites, ricochets of unattributed gems,
accumulating a sense of time-honoured legitimacy along the way, now appears
all at once—fully formed, and therefore faintly suspect.

It is not that the result is more artificial. It is that the process is harder
to romanticise—film noir becomes film now.

For all we know, the anxiety surrounding AI in Hollywood—the sense that
something essential is being lost—may in fact be a form of belated
recognition. From Sunset Boulevard onwards, the industry has always been
preoccupied with its own decline, its own fading sense of reality. AI does not
resolve that anxiety. If anything, it only intensifies it.

Not because it replaces creativity, but because it reveals how much of it had
already become merely procedural.

It feels now as though that first meeting around the table never ended. The
same pauses. The same nods. The same half-finished sentences dressed up as
decisions. People still leaning forward as though something important has just
been said.

Only now the machinery can generate the next version instantly.

Another script treatment. Another pitch. Another recombination of things
everyone already knows.

The room still behaves as though it matters enormously.

But the conviction is thinner now. You will no doubt be able to hear it in the
silence afterwards.
